ready1_open_rewrite.title: SciVerse open question
ready1_open_rewrite.rewritten_question_text: Mitochondria may have originated from symbiosis between ancient anaerobic eukaryotic cells and early bacteria. In the long process of evolution, the symbiotic relationship between the two became closer, and most of the genetic information of the symbiont was transferred to the nucleus, thereby greatly reducing the genetic information on the mitochondria; this is the endosymbiotic theory of mitochondrial origin (shown in the diagram). Much evidence supports this hypothesis: the mitochondrial genetic system is similar to that of bacteria, such as DNA being circular and not bound to histones; the protein synthesis mode of mitochondria is similar to that of bacteria, such as ribosomes being 70S and mechanisms that inhibit protein synthesis, etc. However, this mechanism also has shortcomings, so some scholars have proposed a non-symbiotic hypothesis.

Therefore this statement is correct.
